procedural_history.impugned_order: Order from the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) in Company Appeal (AT) No. 222 of 2018, decided on 25.03.2019.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) heard Company Appeal (AT) No. 222 of 2018. The company (respondent No. 1) opposed interim reliefs, arguing the appellants weren't members, were seeking rectification of the register, and that the petition was time-barred because it was filed on 09.11.2018, more than three years after the alleged share acquisition on 18.04.2015.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging the NCLAT's order. The Supreme Court heard Civil Appeal Nos. 5735-5736 of 2023 and allowed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Petition filed is well within the time.

facts: The respondents raised the issue of limitation, arguing that the appellants claimed to have acquired shares on 18.04.2015 but only filed the company petition on 09.11.2018, which is after the three-year limitation period.
The appellants, in their rejoinder, asserted that their petition was filed within the time limit.
A lower authority, the Acting President, had previously concluded that the petition was not filed within the limitation period.
law: The court noted a prior observation from the NCLT that limitation is a mixed question of law and fact which requires a full examination.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed how the lower authority (the Acting President) handled the limitation issue.
It found the lower authority's decision on this point to be a "bald" summary and a "cryptic approach."
The Court criticized the lower authority for failing to properly examine the issue, especially since it was identified as a mixed question of law and fact.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue of whether the petition was filed within the time limit. Instead, it found the lower court's analysis of the issue to be insufficient and flawed. Consequently, it set aside the lower court's judgment and sent the entire case back to the National Company Law Tribunal for a fresh consideration of all issues, including limitation, on their merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the amount purportedly paid should be treated as consideration to the shareholders of the Company, by the Petitioners.

facts: A lower court, presided over by an Acting President, examined whether money transferred to respondent No. 2's account was for the purchase of shares.
The Acting President noted there was no covering letter or correspondence to support the claim that the payment was for shares.
A discrepancy in the sale consideration amount was observed.
The involvement of a third party, L. Ramesh, was also noted, with the respondent claiming other transactions were involved.

Another lower court order ('impugned order') also found that the transaction did not seem to be a clear payment for shares, citing the involvement of L. Ramesh and the fact that a large sum of money was given and then partially taken back.
application: The Acting President of the lower court surmised that there were other transactions between the parties and concluded that it could not be accepted that the money transferred was for the purchase of shares.
The Supreme Court, in its commentary on the lower court's decision, criticized this reasoning.

The Supreme Court pointed out that the lower court's conclusion was based on "surmise" and that the respondent's version of events should have been required to be proved, rather than being accepted "in this abrupt and self-serving manner."
reasoning.conclusion: The provided text does not state how the Supreme Court ultimately decided this issue. It only explains the reasoning of the lower court and criticizes that court's methodology for reaching its conclusion without sufficient proof. The Supreme Court did not make its own final determination on whether the payment constituted consideration for the shares.

issue.issue_text: Whether the share certificates purportedly issued to the Petitioners are genuine.

facts: The appellants (Petitioners) produced original share certificates to support their claim of being shareholders.
The respondents contended that these certificates were fabricated and not genuine.
The appellants filed applications for the production of the company's original records (shareholder records, Board Resolutions, etc.) to prove the certificates' authenticity.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the decision of the lower court's Acting President on this issue.
The Court noted that the Acting President had concluded the certificates were not genuine, opining that their appearance was "dubious" and the numbers were different.
However, the Supreme Court found that this conclusion was reached superficially, as the Acting President explicitly stated he decided the matter "without going deep into the aspect."
The Supreme Court criticized this approach, stating that "no evidence whatsoever was led or considered on the issue."
The Court emphasized that the genuineness of the documents required verification and they could not be dismissed without the lower court even attempting to do so.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not make a final ruling on whether the share certificates were genuine. Instead, it concluded that the lower court failed to properly decide the issue, as it dismissed the certificates as not genuine without conducting a proper investigation or considering the evidence that was available.

issue.issue_text: Whether any relief can be granted to the Petitioners or whether the petition is maintainable.

facts: The petitioners (appellants) filed a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement.
The respondent company challenged the maintainability of the petition.
The company argued that the petitioners were not members of the company, that the claimed share transfer was invalid, and therefore they lacked the standing (locus) to file the petition.
The company also raised the issue of limitation, stating the petition was filed more than three years after the alleged share acquisition.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the arguments and the decisions of the lower courts.
The Court allowed the appeals, which means it disagreed with the lower courts' dismissal of the petition.

By setting aside the judgments of the lower courts and restoring the company petition to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), the Supreme Court implicitly rejected the preliminary objections regarding maintainability.
The Court directed the NCLT to consider the petition afresh "on merits and in accordance with law, upon proper appreciation of evidence."

This action indicates that the Supreme Court found the petition to be maintainable and deserving of a full hearing on its substantive claims, rather than being dismissed on preliminary grounds like standing or limitation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the petition was maintainable. It allowed the appeals, set aside the lower court orders that had dismissed the case, and remanded the matter back to the National Company Law Tribunal for a fresh decision on the merits.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The exercise of power under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, requires a proper verification of the parties' assertions through an examination of the material, evidence, and facts on record. Questions of fact must be decided on the principle of preponderance of probabilities to reach a conclusion that a reasonable person, acquainted with the relevant field, would draw from the same facts.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) failed to discharge the mandate of law by summarily dismissing the petition without a proper verification of the assertions made by the parties. The exercise of power under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, requires an examination of material, evidence, and facts in right earnest, which was not done. Instead, a narrow view was taken without requiring the respondent to prove their contrary story, despite evidence of them receiving money. The NCLT should have examined the underlying facts, including the receipt of monies and the signatures on transfer deeds, and decided the questions of fact based on the principle of preponderance of probabilities, but it failed to do so.
legal_tests_applied: Exercise of power under Section 59 of the Act of 2013 is to be undertaken in right earnest by examining the material, evidence, and the facts on record.

Questions of fact must be decided on the principle of preponderance of probabilities, giving due weight to the specific facts, as found, so as to draw the conclusion that a reasonable person, acquainted with the relevant field, would draw on the basis of the same facts.

The phrase ‘sufficient cause’ in Section 59 of the Act of 2013 is to be tested in relation to the statutory mandate thereof, i.e., anything done or omitted to be done in contravention of the Act of 2013 or the Rules framed thereunder.
policy_considerations: Specialized tribunals, like the NCLT, have a duty to conduct a proper and thorough inquiry into the facts and evidence presented ('proper verification of the assertions made by the parties was a sine qua non') rather than opting for summary dismissals, ensuring that disputes are resolved on their merits and in accordance with the law.
